entries.title: Future of ARCH2 uncertain amid funding cuts
entries.summary: The Appalachian hydrogen hub is now on the DOE’s list of potential grant cuts, casting doubt on its clean energy future.
entries.content:
A regional project once lauded by federal and state leaders to help achieve a common goal of energy dominance is facing an uncertain future as the Trump administration continues axing federal funding.

The project — called the Appalachian Regional Clean Hydrogen Hub, also known as ARCH2 — was part of the Biden administration’s strategy to achieve its goal of reducing carbon and other greenhouse gas emissions in the power sector. It was one of seven hydrogen hubs across the nation selected in 2023 by the federal government to receive nearly $1 billion in funding.

In 2024, the Appalachian project, along with two other hydrogen hubs, was awarded funding for the first phase of the projects. But since then, the U.S. Department of Energy hasn’t awarded any more money. Instead, the Trump administration rescinded $2.2 billion in funding for two of the hydrogen hubs earlier this year.

The remaining five hydrogen projects, including the Appalachian-based hub, were spared in that round of cuts. However, they may soon be on the chopping block.

In October, it was reported that the federal agency was planning to cancel hundreds of additional grants awarded under the Biden administration. Several news outlets obtained and confirmed a DOE list that identified more than 600 energy grants for termination, including the remaining five hydrogen hubs.

The cancellation of more than 300 of those grants were announced earlier that month. The remaining grants listed, including the hydrogen hubs, have not yet been announced.

The Department of Energy has not confirmed the authenticity of the list or the cancellation of those projects. But it hasn’t completely denied them, either. Instead, the federal agency has said it hasn’t made any other decisions except for what’s already been announced. The DOE did not respond to questions.

The potential loss of funding has added to the confusion around the status of ARCH2.

“The hub’s kind of gone dark,” said Tom Torres, hydrogen program director for the Ohio River Valley Institute. “There’s been very few statements from any of the companies involved.”

So far, project developers have only spent about $2.2 million of the $30 million the project received in 2024, according to government spending data. That initial amount is supposed to fund the project’s first phase where developers intended to “conduct planning, analysis, and design activities in addition to ongoing stakeholder and community engagement across West Virginia, Ohio, and Pennsylvania,” according to the DOE website.

While developers held an open house in West Virginia last November and one in Ohio and Pennsylvania each in January, there haven’t been any more community outreach events since then.

The disbursement of funding has paused for ARCH2, according to Hope Gas spokesperson Christine Mitchell. Hope Gas is one of the ten project development partners.

“While our work with ARCH2 is also paused, Hope Gas continues to look at opportunities for the future of energy in West Virginia that began with the ARCH2 project,” she added.

Mitchell couldn’t confirm whether the pause affected the money already given to the project as Hope Gas wasn’t directly involved in the funding. She deferred such questions to Battelle Memorial Institute, which is the recipient of the ARCH2 DOE funding and one of the managers of the project. Battelle did not respond to questions.

Plug Power, another one of the project’s partners, “remains a project development partner, and is progressing through the first phase accordingly,” Jose Luis Crespo, the company’s president and chief revenue officer, said in an email.

ARCH2 is supposed to create a regional network of facilities across West Virginia, Ohio and Pennsylvania that will produce, store, distribute and utilize hydrogen. In addition to state and local governments, the project has also partnered with a variety of private companies, including Hope Gas and EQT.

At one point, developers were proposing at least 12 projects across West Virginia, Ohio and Pennsylvania to help accelerate hydrogen production and technologies as well as build out the necessary infrastructure. However, the exact locations of those facilities have never been announced, so it’s not clear how many were slated for West Virginia.

The lack of public details, including precise locations for the proposed facilities, has been a major contention point with West Virginia residents and other critics of the project. ARCH2’s website states that potential project sites are currently “under evaluation” and will be “determined following extensive analysis of many factors, including community and stakeholder inputs.”

Last November, four development partners had backed out of the Appalachian hydrogen hub, and one-third of the original 15 projects had been scrapped. And although project representatives said they intended to replace the developers and projects, there’s no indication that they have done so.
